personas.why: I stay to see how the system handles a bad call. The switch from STOP to CHECK FOOTAGE is the part that makes the diagram worth saving.
One STOP in 23 gets my attention. I want to know what made that set cross the line; the boxes tell me where the data went, not where the line was.
The swing is recognisable enough that a friend comes to mind. Then the countdown feels like the start of a different reel, and I scroll instead of sending.
I can see the short rep once the green outline appears. By the gym-buddy replay I've seen the mistake three times and don't have a new question.
I follow the footage and the plain explanation about swinging. When the tiles land, I'm trying to distinguish HOLD from CHECK FOOTAGE for sets I haven't seen.
The skeleton lock-on gets me past the countdown. Seeing it fail when the lifter turns makes this more interesting than a pose-tracking demo; I'd send it to a project teammate.
Comparing against a personal best is a clear idea, and the lunge shows how that comparison can mislead. Once the second check resolves it, I know what the crunch verdict will be.
The false positive earns my attention. Two models agreeing explains why the system issued STOP, but not why the set should never have been done. The last stamp doesn't settle that.
The lunge gives me a concrete example for the diagram: the numbers flag it, the video doesn't, so it goes to review. I'd save that frame to explain the idea to a colleague.
Who gets to overrule the first call is a better question than how many joints it tracks. I stay for that answer; returning to the crunch feels like hearing the conclusion twice.
The ghost makes the hook work even without sound. At the countdown I still have no hint that the AI made a mistake, so there's little reason to wait through a title reveal.
The red tile expanding into the offending rep is an image I'd remember. I can repeat 'my own best, not a textbook' without following the rest of the flowchart, so I move on.
CHECK FOOTAGE is more interesting to me than STOP: there's an actual fallback when the inputs disagree. I'd comment FORM to inspect the coach instructions rather than infer them from the animation.
The camera turn is the best evidence in the reel: the apparent knee depth changes with viewpoint. I'd save the diagram to compare the two judges' inputs, not take their agreement as ground truth.
I'd show someone the ghost and the turned lunge because both are visible on the rep. When the footage gives way to judge and coach boxes, I'd rather see one controlled crunch beside the swung one.
The chant into the skeleton reveal is fun enough to keep me there. The next screen asks me to read a pipeline when what I want to watch is the skeleton follow the lifter.
